items.q: Which statement about a bacterial cell is correct?
items.correct: Its genetic material is a single DNA loop.
items.misconception: Its genetic material is held inside a nucleus.
items.why: Students meet plant and animal cells first, where the nucleus is the most obvious structure, so they treat it as a part that every cell must have. Diagrams of bacteria often show the DNA loop as a dark region that looks like a nucleus. Bacterial cells (prokaryotic cells) have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall. The genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus: it is a single DNA loop and there may be one or more small rings of DNA called plasmids.
items.random_wrong: Its cell wall is made from cellulose fibres.

items.q: A cheek cell is 6 × 10⁻⁵ m wide and a bacterial cell is 2 × 10⁻⁶ m wide. About how many times wider is the cheek cell?
items.why: Textbook diagrams of bacterial cells and animal cells are each drawn to fill the space available, and are usually printed without a scale bar, so the difference in scale is hidden. Bacterial cells (prokaryotic cells) are much smaller in comparison with plant and animal cells. The difference is best shown by an order of magnitude calculation, using standard form.

items.q: A muscle cell contains large numbers of mitochondria. What is the function of these mitochondria?
items.misconception: To make the energy for contraction
items.why: Mitochondria are often described as making or producing energy, and students have not yet separated the idea of energy being transferred from the idea of energy being created and stored. Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place. Respiration transfers energy from glucose so that the cell can use it; the energy is not made in the mitochondria and is not stored there. Cells that need a great deal of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.
items.random_wrong: To join amino acids into new proteins

items.q: Which parts are found in most animal cells?
items.misconception: Cytoplasm, ribosomes and a cellulose wall
items.why: Students learn that a cell wall strengthens the cell and assume every cell needs strengthening. They also learn that bacterial cells have a cell wall, and assume that all cell walls must be made of the same material. Plant and algal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall. Bacterial cells are surrounded by a cell wall, but it is not made of cellulose.

items.q: Which statement about plant cells is correct?
items.correct: Their cell walls are made of cellulose.
items.misconception: Their cell walls are found in animals too.
items.why: Students learn that a cell wall strengthens the cell and assume every cell needs strengthening. They also learn that bacterial cells have a cell wall, and assume that all cell walls must be made of the same material. Plant and algal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall. Bacterial cells are surrounded by a cell wall, but it is not made of cellulose.
items.random_wrong: Their chloroplasts are in every plant cell.

items.q: A plant cell is 0.06 mm long. On a drawing of the cell, the nucleus is about one tenth of the length of the cell. What is the best estimate of the real diameter of the nucleus?
items.why: Students compare the digits in the index (6 against 5) without taking the minus sign into account, and they are used to a bigger digit meaning a bigger number. In standard form the more negative the index, the smaller the number: 10⁻⁶ m is one tenth of 10⁻⁵ m. Order of magnitude calculations should be set out in standard form so that the powers of ten can be compared directly.

items.q: Root hair cells have a long, thin extension that reaches out into the soil. How does this help the cell to carry out its function?
items.correct: It increases the surface area for absorption.
items.misconception: It makes the cell larger so it can work faster.
items.why: Specialised cells are recognised in diagrams by their outline and size, so students focus on the shape of the cell rather than on the sub-cellular structures inside it. As a cell differentiates it acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function. It has become a specialised cell.
items.random_wrong: It exposes the chloroplasts to extra sunlight.

items.q: Which statement about cell differentiation is correct?
items.correct: Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage.
items.misconception: Most plant cells differentiate at an early stage.
items.why: Students learn the pattern for animal cells first and apply it to every organism, without noticing that the specification separates plants from animals here. Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage, whereas many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
items.random_wrong: Most cells differentiate by growing to a bigger size.

items.q: In a mature animal, what is cell division mainly used for?
items.correct: Cell division is for repairing and replacing cells.
items.misconception: Cell division has stopped in mature animals.
items.why: Cell division is introduced as the way organisms grow, so students tie it to growth alone and expect it to stop when growth stops. In mature animals, cell division is mainly restricted to repair and replacement.
items.random_wrong: Cell division makes the cells grow larger.

items.q: Why can an electron microscope be used to study cells in much finer detail than a light microscope?
items.correct: It has more magnification and resolution.
items.misconception: It magnifies the image very many more times.
items.why: Magnification is the quantity students calculate, so it is the familiar idea; resolution is not calculated and is easily left out of the explanation. An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope. This means that it can be used to study cells in much finer detail, and it has enabled biologists to see and understand many more sub-cellular structures.
items.random_wrong: It finds the real size from the image size.

items.q: The image of a cell is 10 mm wide. The real cell is 0.05 mm wide. What is the magnification?
items.why: Students remember that magnification makes things larger and so multiply by it, instead of rearranging magnification = size of image / size of real object. magnification = size of image / size of real object, so size of real object = size of image / magnification. The image size and the real size must be measured in the same units.

items.q: Does every plant cell contain chloroplasts?
items.correct: No. Plant cells often have chloroplasts, but cells that receive no light, such as root hair cells, do not.
items.misconception: Every plant cell contains chloroplasts, because the whole plant carries out photosynthesis.
items.why: The plant cell in almost every diagram is a leaf cell packed with chloroplasts, so students treat chloroplasts as a defining feature of all plant cells rather than as a structure related to a function. In addition to the parts found in animal cells, plant cells often have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis, so cells that are not exposed to light do not contain them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which sub-cellular structure is the site of protein synthesis?
items.misconception: Ribosomes are where respiration takes place, and mitochondria are where the cell's proteins are made.
items.why: Both are small structures in the cytoplasm that are learned as a pair, and their names are unfamiliar, so students swap the two functions. Ribosomes are where protein synthesis takes place; mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place. Each of the main sub-cellular structures has to be related to its own function.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do animal cells contain a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap?
items.correct: No. A permanent vacuole filled with cell sap is one of the parts found in plant cells.
items.misconception: Animal cells contain a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, just as plant cells do.
items.why: The vacuole is such a large and prominent feature of the plant cell diagram that students remember it as a general part of any cell rather than as a plant cell feature. Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. In addition to these parts, plant cells often have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
